thread.title: What Tootsie's Price Really Implies - Tootsie Roll Industries Inc. (NYSE:TR)

author: Stefan Kraguljac Larsen
title: What Tootsie's Price Really Implies - Tootsie Roll Industries Inc. (NYSE:TR)

organizations.name: price really implies - tootsie roll industries inc.

text:
Nobody has missed the fact that Tootsie Roll Industries (NYSE: TR ) is trading at a PE ratio higher than that of some of the most talked about and beloved tech giants like Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL ). A superficial look may indicate a rich valuation, but is there a strong enough valuation case to consider doing something like shorting the stock?
Caretaker Management The 10-K business section, typically the place where the merits of a company are elaborated, is extremely sparse in Tootsie's case. Just over a page long, it makes general remarks about the competitiveness of the confectionery sector and the regional composition of its revenues which are dominated by the US to the point where, as quoted from the 10-K:
The majority of production from the Company’s Canadian plants is sold in the United States.
No concrete mention of the development of growth initiatives can be found. The only time R&D is mentioned is the following as quoted from the 10-K.
Although the Company does research and develops new products and product line extensions for existing brands, it also improves the quality of existing products, improves and modernizes production processes, and develops and implements new technologies to enhance the quality and reduce the costs of products. The Company does not expend material amounts of money on research or development activities.
They actually make an outright statement about how insignificant of a cost item R&D is, not even being visible as a separate line on the income statement. This does not bode well for the quality and frequency of either product of manufacturing innovation, and isn't necessarily something that one has to accept from confectionery companies, especially on the product side. One frequently walks into stores to see all sorts of iterations of the classic brands, like all the variations of Snickers including hazelnut, almond, fudge, cruncher and peanut butter.
When you look at the situation of the management, it is understandable how this blatant disinterest in growth may have come about. The company's current CEO is Ellen Gordon, who was made CEO three years ago when the previous CEO, who also happened to be her 95 year old husband, Melvis Gordon, sadly died. With no disrespect to the elderly, an octogenarian executive does not need to worry about her position or the position of her company in 10 to 15 years time, especially when in the meantime she alone is taking home 5.5 million dollars in compensation a year, which is not insubstantial as more than 1% of the company's total annual revenue. On top of that, the proxy statement reveals that 900,000 dollars was spent on private jet transport and an additional apartment for the CEO, excused as an additional office. These are the sort of special transactions that characterise many of the short sale case studies in Kathryn Staley's book The Art of Short Selling, and are a strong signal of lack of management credibility.
Beyond the fact that there is a lack of top management incentive, who cumulatively take home over 11.3 million dollars in total annual compensation from a stagnating business (which is concerning on its own), there is clearly no reason to expect or value the company for growth. This justifies an expectations valuation of the stock based on the growing perpetuity method.
What Tootsie's market price implies Although price to earnings multiples can be helpful in ball-parking a valuation, I prefer expectations valuation as a framework to understand whether a stock's price is reasonable or not. With some basic assumptions we can use the stock price which contains valuable, implicit data about investor expectations of future cash flows, and disassemble it to see the growth expectations of investors. Since there is no reason to expect any extraordinary growth in cash flows from this company, i.e growth greater than the company's cost of capital, we can simplify the expectations valuation by using the growing perpetuity method.
The Cash Flow
To carry out the analysis of how much growth the market expects in the cash flows to shareholders in perpetuity, we need to find an appropriate value to represent today's cash flow. Since we've assumed that management is not making any effort to improve the company's growth prospects, we'll use NOPAT as the free cash flow to investors, since it is safe to assume that incremental investments in fixed and working capital shouldn't be necessary to keep the business working in its current state. To find NOPAT for this year, we need to multiply today's sales by the operating margin (which is equal to operating profit divided by sales) and by (1 - cash tax rate), which we will proxy conservatively (since this is a short candidate) with the 21% tax rate for corporations post TCJA.
Sales 515674.000 Operating Profit 70905.175 NOPAT 56015.088 Operating Margin 0.138 We get a NOPAT of around 56 million dollars.
Weighted Average Cost of Capital ( WACC)
Tootsie has a D/E ratio of 0.01, so for simplicity the debt weighting will be assumed negligible, and we will discount the NOPAT in our growing perpetuity calculation at the cost of equity shown below.
Cost of Equity 0.055 Risk Free Rate 0.029 Market Premium 0.055 Beta 0.480 The beta of 0.48 is sourced from Investors Business Daily, the risk free rate is the risk free return on 10-year government securities as of today, and the market risk premium used (always a controversial choice) was 5.5% as of the KPMG study on implied risk premia for 2018.
Other Adjustments
Since the growing perpetuity method using NOPAT will give us the corporate value, we need to adjust it to get shareholder value (market cap) by adding non-operating assets and subtracting debt, employee stock options, unfunded balance of the pension plan and post-retirement healthcare benefits.
Nonoperating Assets 138326.00 Debt and Other 116523.00 Its non-operating assets include cash, liquid securities, investments and a line item called restricted cash for a total of 138 million dollars, and its debt, which was only a small bank loan, and the other relevant liabilities totaled around 116.5 million dollars.
Results
By trial-and-error, we can find the growth rate that gives a present value of the growing perpetuity such that, after adjustments, we get the company's current market capitalisation.
The growing perpetuity is the following formula, with the constant g representing the market implied growth expectations for the NOPAT in perpetuity.
To get a valuation for the company at the current market cap of 2.11 billion dollars for Tootsie, the market expects a growth rate (g) of 2.75%, which gives a present value for the growing perpetuity of 2.10 billion dollars, which post adjustments gives just about 2.11 billion dollars in market cap.
PV of Growing Perpetuity 2091406.4 Corporate Value 2091406.4 Nonoperating Assets 138326 Debt and Other 116523 SHAREHOLDER VALUE (in billions) 2.11 A growth rate of 2.75% annually is not impossible for a company to achieve, since it is after all lower than the latest reported figures for the inflation rate. But given the fact that there isn't much reason to expect a secular increase in demand for candy either, with eating culture in the US becoming more prudent with respect to calorie and sugar intake, and the lack of executive incentive to create growth opportunities for Tootsie, an expectation of 2.75% perpetual NOPAT growth is quite demanding. The generation that are familiar with the Tootsie brand are fading away, with the new generation preferring the novelty offered by other brands like Reese's.
Risks if you're planning to short Even though the 2.75% growth of NOPAT in perpetuity is a fairly high expectation from a company with no secular nor individual drivers for growth, shorting this company carries subtantial risks.
The first risk is that if Ellen Gordon dies and a new executive takes over with some ideas to innovate on its existing product lines or implement some new marketing initiatives, the valuation can be much more justified.
The second risk is that even if the company never grows again, you only have a 50% upside. Many short sellers, like the late Joe Feshbach, would only ever short a stock if there was a conceivable 50% upside. Whether no growth in perpetuity is conceivable to you should temper your decision to go through with a short of Tootsie.
The third risk is that the potential decline in stock price may be limited by the fact that TR is a dividend paying stock. Although the academic community would scoff at the idea that payout policy can command a premium, it has happened on rare occasions that delivering a cash income to investors has actually sustained a premium when markets were not as competitive as they should have been. Distortions caused by the fact that it pays dividends does increase the risk that the stock may not decline before substantial changes take place that turn around the prospects of the company.
The fourth risk is that the company's financial health isn't a disaster. They have positive operating cash flows and are fairly GAAP profitable. They also don't have much debt, with a D/E ratio of 1%. What is strange is the massive 22 million dollar operating outflow that suddenly occurred due to an increase in prepaid expenses and other assets , driven primarily by a balooning in prepaids by a factor of 2.1, on the most recent annual cash flow statement. These dramatic changes can often be a precursor to financial gimmickry and earnings management. But besides that anomaly, and an unsettling decline in net product sales, the company going bust is not going to be part of the short thesis, which for many short sellers is necessary to justify the risk.
The last risk is that the model I used to find the implicit expectations of the growth of Tootsie's cash flows may be flawed in some way. The use of the growing perpetuity method makes the model sensitive, since a growing perpetuity is usually an assumption made for the horizon value, which is also discounted rather heavily into the present under normal circumstances. Also the choice of equity premium could be considered controversial by some, although in the context of my analysis, using a rather low market premium, at least lower than those based on long term historical data, is conservative.
Conclusion Although there is not a strong recent history for growth, with sales declining an average of 2% a year in the last 3 years, and no concrete reason to expect this downward trend to change, a 2.75% perpetual growth in NOPAT is not totally unreasonable. For investors that are confident that the Tootsie valuation is something that markets have missed, and think that the executives are destroying value and will continue to allow loss of market share and sales, take the opportunity to proceed with the short, but even if they end up never growing again, you only have a 50% upside.
Disclosure: I am/we are short TR.
